'''Deborah Charlesworth''' {{post-nominals|country=GBR|FRS|FRSE}} (née Maltby; born 1943) is a [[Population genetics|population geneticist]] from the [[United Kingdom|UK]], notable for her important discoveries in [[population genetics]] and [[evolutionary biology]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last1=Mable|first1=Barbara|last2=Hill|first2=Bill|date=February 2008|title=editorial|journal=Genetics Research|language=en|volume=90|issue=1|pages=1|doi=10.1017/S0016672307009093|issn=1469-5073|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Deborah Charlesworth {{!}} Royal Society|url=https://royalsociety.org/people/deborah-charlesworth-11206/|access-date=2020-11-19|website=royalsociety.org|language=en-gb}}</ref> Her most notable research is in understanding the evolution of [[Homologous recombination|recombination]], [[sex chromosome]]s and mating system for plants.<ref name=":0" />

== Early life and education ==
Charlesworth grew up in a [[London]] suburb, and from a young age was very interested in the natural world around her.<ref name="genetres" />

Although Charlesworth initially studied biochemistry, genetic variation played a significant role from the beginning her research.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|date=2012|title=Recipient of the 2011 Molecular Ecology Prize: Deborah Charlesworth|journal=Molecular Ecology|language=en|volume=21|issue=1|pages=23–25|doi=10.1111/j.1365-294X.2011.05385.x|pmid=22181850|issn=1365-294X|last1=Wright|first1=S.|s2cid=28511114|doi-access=free}}</ref> Charlesworth obtained her doctorate at [[University of Cambridge|Cambridge University]] in 1968 with her thesis focusing on the quantitative genetics of mice, specifically the extent of genetic variation in the blood glucose levels across natural strains.<ref name=":2" />

==Research career==

Charlesworth continued her research at [[University of Cambridge|Cambridge]] and Chicago as a research fellow in human genetics examining amino acid variations in hemoglobins in human populations.<ref name=":2" /> Charlesworth's interest in evolutionary biology continued through her collaboration with [[Brian Charlesworth]], specifically their works on mimicry systems and recombination rates causing her to shift her focus to evolution.<ref name=":2" /> She continued her post-doctoral research at, [[University of Chicago]], [[University of Liverpool]] and [[University of Sussex]] as [[Brian Charlesworth]] took positions at each, causing her to do research without financial support.<ref name=":2" /> She was mentored at Cambridge by [[Hermann Lehmann]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|title=Evolution Tree - Deborah Charlesworth|url=https://academictree.org/evolution/peopleinfo.php?pid=58687|access-date=2020-11-23|website=academictree.org}}</ref>

From 1988 - 1997, at the age of 45, Charlesworth obtained her first faculty position, teaching at [[University of Chicago]].<ref name="genetres" /> By this time, Charlesworth had already published ~50 articles.<ref name=":2" /> Charlesworth was then appointed to a Professorial Research Fellowship at the [[University of Edinburgh]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.ed.ac.uk/biology|title=Biological Sciences|website=The University of Edinburgh}}</ref>

She is best known for her work on the evolution of genetic self-incompatibility in plants and is recognised as a leader in that field. According to the [[Web of Science]] she has published over 300 articles in [[peer-reviewed journal]]s. These articles have been cited over 10,000 times and she has an [[h-index]] of 53.<ref>{{Cite web
  | title = Web of Science
  | year = 2008
  | url = http://isiwebofknowledge.com
  | access-date = 24 August 2008
  }}</ref> She has been married since 1967 to the British evolutionary biologist [[Brian Charlesworth]], who she ended up working in population genetics with.<ref name="genetres" />

==Awards and honors==
Charlesworth was elected a [[Fellow]] of the [[Royal Society of Edinburgh]] in 2001<ref name="genetres">{{cite journal|last=Mable|first=Barbara|author2=Hill Bill|date=February 2008|title=Deborah Charlesworth|journal=Genet. Res.|volume=90|issue=1|pages=1|doi=10.1017/S0016672307009093|pmid=18509956|doi-access=free}}</ref> and a [[List of Fellows of the Royal Society elected in 2005|Fellow of the Royal Society (FRS) in 2005]].<ref name="royalsoc">{{cite web|url=https://royalsociety.org/people/deborah-charlesworth-11206/|title=EC/1991/08: Charlesworth, Deborah|publisher=The Royal Society}}</ref>
In 2011, Charlesworth was awarded the Molecular Ecology Prize.<ref>{{Cite journal|date=2012|title=Recipient of the 2011 Molecular Ecology Prize: Deborah Charlesworth|journal=Molecular Ecology|language=en|volume=21|issue=1|pages=23–25|doi=10.1111/j.1365-294X.2011.05385.x|pmid=22181850|issn=1365-294X|last1=Wright|first1=S.|s2cid=28511114|doi-access=free}}</ref> Charlesworth was awarded the Genetics Society Medal 2019.<ref name="gensoc">{{cite web | url=https://www.genetics.org.uk/medals-and-prizes/genetics-society-medals-and-lectures/genetics-society-medal/genetics-society-medal-2019-deborah-charlesworth/ | title=Genetics Society}}</ref> She was awarded 
a Lifetime Achievement Award by the [[Society for the Study of Evolution]] in January 2020.<ref name="SSE2020">{{cite web |title=Awards & Grants: 2020 Lifetime Achievement Award Recipient |url=http://www.evolutionsociety.org/news/display/2020/1/27/2020-lifetime-achievement-award-recipient/ |website=Society for the Study of Evolution |access-date=29 January 2020 |archive-date=27 March 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210327205131/https://fonts.googleapis.com/css?family=Source+Sans+Pro:200,200i,300,300i,400,400i,600,600i,700,700i,900,900i |url-status=dead }}</ref>
In 2022, she was elected to the [[National Academy of Sciences]].<ref name="naselection">{{Cite web|title=2022 NAS Election|url=https://www.nasonline.org/news-and-multimedia/news/2022-nas-election.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220503174757/http://www.nasonline.org/news-and-multimedia/news/2022-nas-election.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=3 May 2022|language=en-gb|access-date=18 June 2022}}</ref>

{{Scholia}}
* Charlesworth, D, Wright, SI. (2001) Breeding systems and genome evolution. Current Opinion in Genetics & Development 11, 685–690.
* Jesper S. Bechsgaard, Vincent Castric, Deborah Charlesworth, Xavier Vekemans, Mikkel H. Schierup. 2006. The transition to self-compatibility in Arabidopsis thaliana and evolution within S-haplotypes over 10 million years. Molecular Biology and Evolution 23: 1741–1750.
* Asher D. Cutter, Scott E. Baird and Deborah Charlesworth. 2006 Patterns of nucleotide polymorphism and the decay of linkage disequilibrium in wild populations of Caenorhabditis remanei. Genetics 174: 901–913.
* Bergero, R., A. Forrest, E. Kamau, and D. Charlesworth. 2007. Evolutionary strata on the X chromosomes of the dioecious plant Silene latifolia: evidence from new sex-linked genes. Genetics 175:1945-1954.
* D. Charlesworth 2006 Balancing selection and its effects on sequences in nearby genome regions. PLoS Genetics 2: e64 DOI: 10.1371/journal.pgen.0020064.
* S. Qiu, R. Bergero, A. Forrest, V. Kaiser, D. Charlesworth 2010 Nucleotide diversity in Silene latifolia autosomal and sex-linked genes. Proceedings of the Royal Soc. 277: 3283-3290 (doi:10.1098/rspb.2010.0606).
* Bergero, R., and D. Charlesworth, 2011 Preservation of the Y transcriptome in a 10MY old plant sex chromosome system. Current Biology 21: 1470–1474.
* Jordan, C., and D. Charlesworth, 2012 The potential for sexually antagonistic polymorphism in different genome regions. Evolution 66: 505–516.
